title: Rajkummar Rao Vanishes Into Ujjwal Nikam — and the 'Prahaar' Teaser Walks Straight Into the Kasab Trial
excerpt: Slipped quietly into Cocktail 2's prints, the first look at Maddock's 26/11 courtroom drama ends on the line every Indian remembers — and the chameleon of Hindi cinema disappears all over again.
body:
There's a particular kind of silence in a cinema when a teaser nobody warned you about begins to play. That's what happened this week to audiences who walked in for the candy-floss froth of Cocktail 2 and were ambushed, mid-popcorn, by something far heavier: a clipped, grey-toned 117 seconds that opens on a courtroom and ends on a sentence that still tightens the chest seventeen years later.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=rPZw29Zh6Oo

That teaser is Prahaar – The Ujjwal Nikam Story, and the man at the centre of it is Rajkummar Rao, doing the thing he does better than almost anyone in Hindi cinema right now — disappearing.

The strategy was pure Maddock cunning. Producer Dinesh Vijan hard-locked the teasers of two of his upcoming films into the prints of Cocktail 2, so a paying romcom crowd became the unwitting first audience for a 26/11 courtroom drama. No midnight digital drop, no countdown — just the lights going down and Rao's voice filling the hall.

"For the crime of waging war against India, I, Ujjwal Nikam, demand that Ajmal Amir Kasab should be hanged till death."

That's how it ends. And in the theatres where it played, people clapped.

Rao plays Ujjwal Nikam, the special public prosecutor who became a household name during the trial of Ajmal Kasab, the lone surviving gunman of the November 2008 Mumbai attacks. The film, the title makes clear, isn't a sprawling career biopic — it zeroes in on the one case that defined him, the case that played out on every television set in the country while the wounds of 26/11 were still raw.

What's striking in the teaser is how little Rao performs and how much he simply becomes. The familiar boy-next-door softness is gone. In its place: a leaner, harder face, a controlled fury, and — the detail everyone is talking about — Marathi diction so clean it lends the whole thing an unnerving authenticity. This is the actor who melted into Newton, into Srikanth, into a dozen men who looked nothing like a movie star. Here he does it again, and the transformation is the entire pitch.

The craft behind the camera matches him. Prahaar is directed by Avinash Arun, the cinematographer-turned-director behind the acclaimed Paatal Lok and Three of Us, a filmmaker who knows exactly how to hold tension in a frame without raising his voice. The supporting bench is stacked: Wamiqa Gabbi, Jaideep Ahlawat, and Sikandar Kher, the kind of ensemble that signals a film with ambitions well beyond the average courtroom procedural. The CBFC cleared the teaser with a U/A 16+ certificate earlier this month.

There's a knowingness to one exchange already doing the rounds — a question about identity met with a single word: "India." It's the sort of line built for the front bench, and it tells you the register the film is aiming for: not subtle, exactly, but stirring, and unafraid of the goosebump moment.

For the diaspora, this one carries weight beyond the usual. 26/11 is the rare Indian tragedy that registered globally — the Taj burning was on the front page of every Western newspaper — and Nikam's name travelled with it. A film that returns to that trial, with an actor of Rao's calibre at the helm, is the kind of serious-minded Hindi cinema that NRI audiences in the US, UK and Canada actively seek out, the antidote to franchise fatigue.

Prahaar – The Ujjwal Nikam Story releases in cinemas on August 7, 2026. A theatrical run almost always means a JioHotstar or Netflix streaming window for international viewers within roughly eight weeks of release, with subtitles — the standard Maddock playbook — so diaspora fans who can't catch it in a multiplex won't wait long.

It arrives in a packed Maddock summer, sharing teaser space with Shraddha Kapoor's Eetha, and into a Bollywood calendar suddenly thick with prestige. But on the evidence of this first look, Prahaar isn't trying to be the loudest film in the room. It's trying to be the one you can't stop thinking about on the drive home. On Rao's track record alone, bet on it pulling that off.
